Most households approaching or living in retirement do not lose sleep—or hard-earned savings—because they ignored the market. They lose both because financial media pushes savers to chase dozens of noisy stock stories at once, quietly drifting into pure technology concentration right before a multi-year downturn.

We built Truth of Market as an independent, strictly non-advisory educational research publisher. Rather than issuing speculative trade alerts, our historical research studies one enduring empirical structure: pairing secular semiconductor innovation (SMH) with non-cyclical healthcare cash flows (XLV) and short-term US Treasury reserves (SGOV).

Use our Historical Sector Backtest Explorer to compare how different 2000–2025 SMH × XLV + SGOV historical study ratios behaved across past downturns, and explore our Educational Market Data Newsletter + 2000–2025 Historical Statistical Workbook.

COMPLIMENTARY EDUCATIONAL REFERENCE ($0)

US Brokerage Limit-Order & ETF Terminology Guide

I. Limit Orders vs. Market Orders
On self-directed platforms such as Fidelity, Charles Schwab, or Vanguard, a Limit Order specifies a maximum purchase price rather than accepting temporary bid-ask spread widening during the first 15 minutes after the 9:30 AM ET open.
II. Non-Leveraged 1x Spot Sector ETFs
Both SMH (Semiconductors) and XLV (US Healthcare) are unleveraged 1x spot ETFs free from daily 3x leveraged volatility-reset decay.
III. Short-Term US Treasury Liquidity Reference
In historical case studies, short-term household reserve buckets are commonly modeled using 0–3 month US Treasury bills (SGOV) or government money-market funds (SPAXX / SWVXX / VMFXX).
